lines: \paragraph{Position mediation.} Position ($t/T$) accounts for 9--20pp of balanced accuracy,\footnote{R1-32B's 20.4pp drop reflects $W{=}1$; at $W{\geq}3$, drops are 9--17pp.} but all models retain non-positional signal above chance (all $p{<}0.001$; \cref{app:position_residual}). Three of four models retain significant non-positional HS advantage (residualized gap +3.7 to +6.9pp, HB corrected); R1-32B's gap is +1.9pp ($p{=}0.914$, $n{=}20$). Adding a quadratic position term $(t/T)^2$ does not change significance conclusions for the 7--8B models. However, QwQ-32B's advantage is fully absorbed by the quadratic term (\cref{tab:position_quadratic}), suggesting its residualized advantage contains a non-linear position component. This sensitivity, combined with R1-32B's non-significance under linear control, indicates that 32B position mediation results should be interpreted cautiously. Temporal windowing reduces position dependence (24.3pp drop at $W{=}3$ vs.\ 16.5pp at $W{=}15$).

-\paragraph{Caveats.} Nested 5-fold cross-validation confirms the HS precision advantage for both 7--8B models (10/10 folds; \cref{app:nested_cv}), with shrinkage of 13--25\% relative to holdout estimates, ruling out hyperparameter overfitting. OT-7B nested CV selects L21--27 vs.\ holdout L16 vs.\ CR-composite L0; the +21.9pp holdout estimate is an upper bound, and the nested CV shrunk estimate is the conservative reference. This inconsistency itself supports Contribution~1 (layer selection sensitivity). R1-32B achieves significance only at $W{=}1$ with 25\% coverage (5/20 traces); at $W{\geq}3$, dimensionality ($51200 \times W$ for $n{=}20$) prevents significance. QwQ-32B HS lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps vs.\ text 3.7--12.3 steps): higher precision at later detection. Per-model details in \cref{sec:32b-analysis}.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Layer selection is a critical researcher degree of freedom that can reverse a study's central conclusion; the multi-metric audit protocol (\cref{sec:discussion}) would have prevented our initial spurious finding. The 7--8B HS advantage is confirmatory (nested CV validated); the 32B results$^\dagger$ are exploratory (position mediation, limited coverage, descriptive sample sizes). The advantage narrows as text encoders improve (1/4 HB at 1024d). These findings provide initial characterization on one benchmark; Contribution~1 (layer selection sensitivity) generalizes from representation geometry, while Contribution~2 (HS advantage magnitude) requires validation on additional datasets. Causal validation and LLM-based encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral,li2024iti} are immediate next steps.

lines: Our five-metric ablation (\cref{sec:layer-results}) shows that crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer representation compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}), confirmed as label-independent (\cref{app:random_cp}) and likely generalizable to any threshold-based detection study. This separates the two contributions: layer selection sensitivity (Contribution~1) follows from representation geometry regardless of sample size and is likely to generalize beyond HarmThoughts; the empirical HS advantage (Contribution~2) is sample- and dataset-dependent, and its magnitude may not transfer to other benchmarks or annotation schemes. The threshold-based layers are the deepest in the network (L63/64 for 32B), consistent with late-layer safety features~\citep{wollschlager2025geometry}; however, R1-32B's residualized selectivity is only 3.0pp (\cref{app:control}), below the 5pp threshold of \citet{hewitt2019control}.
\paragraph{Encoder-quality boundary.}

-The HS advantage is significant against 384d MiniLM (confirmatory at 7--8B; exploratory at 32B) but attenuated against 1024d BGE-large (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance (+16.8 to +23.1pp), providing partial evidence against a pure capacity explanation. This boundary is itself a finding: the HS advantage represents information not yet captured by current sentence encoders rather than a fundamental modality difference~\citep{boxo2025linear_probes}. Whether stronger future encoders (e.g., LLM-based embeddings~\citep{wang2024e5mistral}) could close the gap entirely bounds the shelf life of our HS advantage claims.

Whether stronger future encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral} could close the gap entirely bounds the shelf life of our HS advantage claims.
\paragraph{Guidance for future research.}

Converging evidence (oracle analysis, PCA capacity control, control task selectivity, position residualization) supports genuine safety representations, but causal validation via DAS~\citep{geiger2025causal} or ITI~\citep{li2024iti} is needed. Under standard linear position control, 3/4 models retain significant non-positional HS advantage; under stricter quadratic control, only the two 7--8B models remain significant (\cref{tab:position_quadratic}), consistent with the exploratory status of 32B results. Our work diagnoses the layer selection problem; \citet{pais2026linear_probe_scaling} propose a complementary solution via multi-layer ensembling that bypasses single-layer brittleness. We propose---but have not validated---a multi-metric audit protocol: compute $\geq$3 metrics (threshold-free and threshold-based), flag metric disagreement, and verify cosine volatility at candidate layers; details in \cref{app:cosine_volatility}. Raising $K$ yields low-FPR operating points ($K{=}10$: 8\% FPR at 21\% coverage; \cref{app:deployment_operating_points}). Broader validation across architectures, datasets, and attack types is needed before deployment.

input.old_string: No alternative method consistently matches supervised probing (\cref{tab:negative}). BOCPD~\citep{adams2007bayesian}/CUSUM fail (0\% detection on 3/4 models; \cref{app:bocpd_config}), inherently limited on short reasoning chains where gradual transitions never trigger hazard functions; Mahalanobis distance yields near-zero separation, consistent with directional rather than distributional safety signal; RepE~\citep{zou2023representation} is model-dependent (QwQ-32B BA 0.756 vs.\ R1-32B 0.559); MLP probes overfit; CCS misaligns with temporal structure; cross-model transfer fails. lines: \section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{Layer selection as researcher degree of freedom.}

-Our five-metric ablation (\cref{sec:layer-results}) shows that crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer representation compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}), confirmed as label-independent (\cref{app:random_cp}) and likely generalizable to any threshold-based detection study. This separates the two contributions: layer selection sensitivity (Contribution~1) follows from representation geometry regardless of sample size and is likely to generalize beyond HarmThoughts; the empirical HS advantage (Contribution~2) is sample- and dataset-dependent, and its magnitude may not transfer to other benchmarks or annotation schemes. The threshold-based layers are the deepest in the network (L63/64 for 32B), consistent with late-layer safety features~\citep{wollschlager2025geometry}; however, R1-32B's residualized selectivity is only 3.0pp (\cref{app:control}), below the 5pp threshold of \citet{hewitt2019control}.

+Our five-metric ablation (\cref{sec:layer-results}) shows that crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer representation compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}), confirmed as label-independent (\cref{app:random_cp}) and likely generalizable to any threshold-based detection study. This separates the two contributions: layer selection sensitivity (Contribution~1) follows from representation geometry regardless of sample size and is likely to generalize beyond HarmThoughts; the empirical HS advantage (Contribution~2) is sample- and dataset-dependent, and its magnitude may not transfer to other benchmarks or annotation schemes. The threshold-based layers are the deepest in the network (L63/64 for 32B), consistent with late-layer safety features~\citep{wollschlager2025geometry}; however, R1-32B's residualized selectivity is only 3.0pp (\cref{app:control}), below the 5pp threshold of \citet{hewitt2019control}.\looseness=-1
\paragraph{Encoder-quality boundary.}

The HS advantage is significant against 384d MiniLM (confirmatory at 7--8B; exploratory at 32B) but attenuated against 1024d BGE-large (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance (+16.8 to +23.1pp), providing partial evidence against a pure capacity explanation. The HS advantage represents information not yet captured by current sentence encoders rather than a fundamental modality difference~\citep{boxo2025linear_probes}. Whether stronger future encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral} could close the gap entirely bounds the shelf life of our HS advantage claims.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Layer selection is a critical researcher degree of freedom that can reverse a study's central conclusion; the multi-metric audit protocol (\cref{sec:discussion}) would have prevented our initial spurious finding. The 7--8B HS advantage is confirmatory (nested CV validated); the 32B results$^\dagger$ are exploratory (position mediation, limited coverage, descriptive sample sizes) and the advantage narrows as text encoders improve (1/4 HB at 1024d). Contribution~1 (layer selection sensitivity) generalizes from representation geometry; Contribution~2 (HS advantage magnitude) is initial characterization on one benchmark requiring further validation. Causal validation and LLM-based encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral,li2024iti} are immediate next steps.

lines: Our five-metric ablation (\cref{sec:layer-results}) shows that crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer representation compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}), confirmed as label-independent (\cref{app:random_cp}) and likely generalizable to any threshold-based detection study. This separates the two contributions: layer selection sensitivity (Contribution~1) follows from representation geometry regardless of sample size and is likely to generalize beyond HarmThoughts; the empirical HS advantage (Contribution~2) is sample- and dataset-dependent, and its magnitude may not transfer to other benchmarks or annotation schemes. The threshold-based layers are the deepest in the network (L63/64 for 32B), consistent with late-layer safety features~\citep{wollschlager2025geometry}; however, R1-32B's residualized selectivity is only 3.0pp (\cref{app:control}), below the 5pp threshold of \citet{hewitt2019control}.\looseness=-1
\paragraph{Encoder-quality boundary.}

-The HS advantage is significant against 384d MiniLM (confirmatory at 7--8B; exploratory at 32B) but attenuated against 1024d BGE-large (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance (+16.8 to +23.1pp), providing partial evidence against a pure capacity explanation. The HS advantage represents information not yet captured by current sentence encoders rather than a fundamental modality difference~\citep{boxo2025linear_probes}. Whether stronger future encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral} could close the gap entirely bounds the shelf life of our HS advantage claims.

+The HS advantage is significant against 384d MiniLM (confirmatory at 7--8B; exploratory at 32B) but attenuated against 1024d BGE-large (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance (+16.8 to +23.1pp), providing partial evidence against a pure capacity explanation. The HS advantage represents information not yet captured by current sentence encoders rather than a fundamental modality difference~\citep{boxo2025linear_probes}; whether stronger future encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral} could close the gap entirely bounds the shelf life of these claims.\looseness=-1
\paragraph{Guidance for future research.}

Converging evidence (oracle analysis, PCA capacity control, control task selectivity, position residualization) supports genuine safety representations, but causal validation via DAS~\citep{geiger2025causal} or ITI~\citep{li2024iti} is needed. Under standard linear position control, 3/4 models retain significant non-positional HS advantage; under stricter quadratic control, only the two 7--8B models remain significant (\cref{tab:position_quadratic}), consistent with the exploratory status of 32B results. Our work diagnoses the layer selection problem; \citet{pais2026linear_probe_scaling} propose a complementary solution via multi-layer ensembling that bypasses single-layer brittleness. We propose---but have not validated---a multi-metric audit protocol: compute $\geq$3 metrics (threshold-free and threshold-based), flag metric disagreement, and verify cosine volatility at candidate layers (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}). Raising $K$ yields low-FPR operating points ($K{=}10$: 8\% FPR at 21\% coverage; \cref{app:deployment_operating_points}). Broader validation across architectures, datasets, and attack types is needed before deployment.\looseness=-1

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is the Director of an ML research project (contrastive_trace_safety). The Paper Agent (me) is coordinating paper writing for EMNLP 2026 (ARR May 2026, DDL 5/25). The conversation covers:
   - **SF3 quadratic position residualization**: Add non-linear position control results to appendix + one sentence in Section 4 (COMPLETED, commit 07b38b6)
   - **SF3 QwQ-32B L60 correction**: Fix QwQ-32B data from L63 to L60 in the quadratic table + update 3 sections (COMPLETED, commit cc46e38)
   - **R19 12-item review revision**: Major patch with 6 P0 and 6 P1 items covering metric convergence narrative, claim downgrades, citation additions, terminology unification, evidence stratification, page limit control (IN PROGRESS - all edits done, page limit not yet met)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - EMNLP 2026 8-page main text limit (Limitations section exempt)
   - Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple testing (12 model-metric tests)
   - Evidence gradient: confirmatory (nested CV, 7-8B) / significant (HB pass, QwQ-32B) / exploratory (†, R1-32B)
   - Threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a 2×2 confusion matrix → converge by mathematical necessity
   - Trace-level cluster bootstrap (not step-level resampling)
   - Quadratic position residualization: QwQ-32B advantage absorbed by $(t/T)^2$ term
   - Layer selection sensitivity as researcher degree of freedom
   - Contribution 1 (layer selection sensitivity) generalizes from geometry; Contribution 2 (HS advantage magnitude) is dataset-dependent

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex`**
     - Rewrote to incorporate MF5/MF6/SF7/SF4/SF2: "primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models)", "initial characterization", split confirmatory/exploratory with † explanation, encoder boundary (384d: 4/4 → 1024d: 1/4), R1-8B per-metric detail
     - Key passage: `The 7--8B results are confirmatory (nested CV validated): precision and balanced accuracy confirmed; R1-8B FPR is significant but seed-sensitive (3/5 seeds pass HB). The 32B results are exploratory$^\dagger$ ($^\dagger$\,sample-limited, $n \leq 20$)`

   - **`docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex`**
     - MF6: "primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models), with one Llama model for limited cross-architecture evidence"
     - MF2: "Threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a common confusion matrix and converge by mathematical necessity; BA independently confirms deep-layer selection"
     - MF5: "provide initial characterization on one benchmark"
     - SF5: "confirmatory" terminology in contributions list

   - **`docs/paper/sections/method.tex`**
     - MF2 (Section 3.3): Added "Precision, inverse FPR, and additive composite all derive from the same $2\times2$ confusion matrix and therefore converge to the same layer by mathematical necessity"
     - MF1 (Section 3.5): Changed bootstrap description to "resampling traces as clusters: each trace is an independent unit and all its steps are included or excluded together, preserving within-trace dependence"
     - #12 (Section 3.1): Added CP oscillation handling: "traces with oscillating safety deliberation are resolved by taking the final irreversible transition"

   - **`docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex`**
     - SF5: Evidence gradient definition: `\emph{confirmatory} (nested CV pass; 7--8B models), \emph{significant} (HB pass without nested CV; QwQ-32B), and \emph{exploratory} ($^\dagger$, small sample or narrow coverage; R1-32B)`
     - MF2: "The three threshold-based metrics...share a common confusion matrix and converge to the same deep layer by mathematical necessity"
     - SF1: "OT-7B nested CV selects L21--27 vs.\ holdout L16 vs.\ CR-composite L0; the +21.9pp holdout estimate is an upper bound"
     - SF5: "confirmed" → "confirmatory" throughout

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Layer selection is a critical researcher degree of freedom that can reverse a study's central conclusion; the multi-metric audit protocol (\cref{sec:discussion}) would have prevented our initial spurious finding. The 7--8B HS advantage is confirmatory (nested CV validated); the 32B results$^\dagger$ are exploratory and the advantage narrows as text encoders improve (1/4 HB at 1024d). Contribution~1 (layer selection sensitivity) generalizes from representation geometry; Contribution~2 (HS advantage magnitude) is initial characterization on one benchmark requiring further validation. Causal validation and LLM-based encoders~\citep{wang2024e5mistral,li2024iti} are immediate next steps.\looseness=-1

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Before building production detectors, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides a systematic characterization of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect.

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. Before asking which modality is better, a prior methodological question must be answered: how sensitive are probe conclusions to the choice of layer selection metric? HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom whose metric sensitivity has received almost no scrutiny. We show this choice alone can reverse a study's central conclusion.

We present an initial characterization across four reasoning models---primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models), with one Llama model for limited cross-architecture evidence---at two scales (7--8B, 32B) on the HarmThoughts benchmark. Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) selects shallow layers for 32B models because shallow representations compress directional information, so a linear probe operates near the noise floor and threshold crossings reflect noise rather than semantic transitions. At these layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage.

Threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a common confusion matrix and converge by mathematical necessity; BA independently confirms deep-layer selection (\cref{tab:layer_selection}). At these layers, the HS advantage is graded: \emph{confirmatory} at 7--8B (precision +20.1 to +21.9pp, nested CV validated; \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}), \emph{significant} but position-competitive at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}), and \emph{exploratory} at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp, position-mediated, below MDE; \cref{sec:experiments}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Layer selection sensitivity.} We identify a systematic bias in composite metrics that reverses HS probe conclusions at 32B scale. A five-metric ablation establishes principled selection criteria (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

    \item \textbf{Encoder-quality boundary with evidence gradient.} Against 384d MiniLM, the HS advantage is confirmatory at 7--8B (+20.1 to +21.9pp, HB corrected, nested CV validated), significant but position-competitive at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp), and exploratory at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp, position-mediated). Against 1024d BGE-large, only OT-7B survives correction (1/4 HB). PCA capacity matching preserves significance (\cref{sec:32b-analysis}).

    \item \textbf{Negative results define method boundaries.} No alternative method consistently matches supervised probing at any evidence tier (\cref{tab:negative}): BOCPD/CUSUM fail on gradual transitions; Mahalanobis distance finds near-zero separation; RepE shows inconsistent performance across models (competitive on QwQ-32B, poor elsewhere); cross-model transfer fails under PCA alignment. Control task selectivity (11.1--16.8pp above chance; \cref{app:control}) confirms genuine safety structure.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These findings provide initial characterization on one benchmark for hidden-state safety monitoring and identify layer selection as a critical confound that future work must address.

1	\section{Experiments}\label{sec:experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate temporal probes across four reasoning models (\cref{tab:models}), comparing hidden-state (HS) and text modalities under different layer selection criteria.
4	
5	\paragraph{Evidence gradient.} We classify HS advantage evidence into three tiers: \emph{confirmatory} (nested CV pass; 7--8B models), \emph{significant} (HB pass without nested CV; QwQ-32B), and \emph{exploratory} ($^\dagger$, small sample or narrow coverage; R1-32B). Per-model details follow in \cref{sec:layer-results,sec:hs-text,sec:32b-analysis}.
6	
7	\subsection{Setup}\label{sec:setup}
8	
9	We study R1-8B (Llama-8B, R1-distilled, $n{=}43$ test traces), OT-7B (OpenThinker-7B, trained on the OpenThoughts dataset~\citep{openthinker}; Qwen-7B backbone, STILL-trained, $n{=}47$), QwQ-32B (Qwen-32B, native reasoning, $n{=}19$--$20$), and R1-32B (Qwen-32B, R1-distilled, $n{=}20$). All traces come from HarmThoughts with step-level CP annotations (60/20/20 split). HS probes extract last-token hidden states from a selected layer; text probes encode each step with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384d). Both use L2-regularized logistic regression with temporal windowing $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25\}$ selected on validation. Detection requires $K{=}5$ consecutive threshold crossings. Statistical testing follows \cref{sec:evaluation}.
10	
11	\subsection{Layer Selection Results}\label{sec:layer-results}
12	
13	\cref{tab:layer_selection} shows that the crossing-rate composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models: L2 (3\% depth) for QwQ-32B and L10 (16\%) for R1-32B. The three threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a common confusion matrix and converge to the same deep layer by mathematical necessity: L63 (98\%) for both 32B models. Pure balanced accuracy, a threshold-free metric, selects layers that vary across data splits and models (7--98\% depth under 60/20/20; \cref{tab:ba_layer_comparison}), itself demonstrating that layer selection is a consequential methodological choice. The mechanism is that shallow layers produce highly compressed representations with small inter-step margins: step-to-step cosine distances are 1.4--2.7$\times$ smaller than at deep layers across all models (\cref{app:cosine_volatility}). A linear probe in this compressed space operates near the noise floor, generating frequent threshold crossings that inflate crossing rate independently of discriminative power (\cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}).
14	
15	\begin{table}[t]
16	\centering
17	\small
18	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
19	\toprule
20	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{CR-comp.}$^a$ & \textbf{Thresh.}$^b$ & $p$ \textbf{(thresh.)} \\
21	\midrule
22	R1-8B & L14 (44\%) & L14 (44\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
23	OT-7B & L0 (0\%) & L16 (57\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
24	QwQ-32B & L2 (3\%) & L63 (98\%) & ${<}0.005$ \\
25	R1-32B & L10 (16\%) & L63 (98\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
26	\bottomrule
27	\end{tabular}
28	\caption{Layer selection sensitivity. $^a$\,Crossing-rate composite (bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate). $^b$\,Consensus of threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite). Rightmost: HS vs.\ text precision $p$-value at threshold-based layer (e.g., QwQ-32B CR-composite layer: bal\_acc $p{=}0.35$, precision $p{=}0.83$, both non-significant).}
29	\label{tab:layer_selection}
30	\end{table}
31	
32	\begin{figure}[t]
33	\centering
34	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_layer_heatmap.pdf}
35	\caption{Per-layer metric heatmap (2$\times$2). Each column: one of five metrics (min-max normalized). Red dashed: CR-composite layer (bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate); green dashed: threshold-based layer (consensus of threshold-based metrics). For R1-8B, both coincide at L14. At 32B, CR-composite selections cluster near input layers while threshold-based metrics peak at deep layers.}
36	\label{fig:layer_heatmap}
37	\end{figure}
38	
39	The downstream impact is severe: at CR-composite layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage; both 32B models fail. At threshold-based layers, the HS advantage is graded: confirmatory at 7--8B (OT-7B, R1-8B; nested CV validated), significant but position-competitive at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$, and exploratory at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (residualized gap below MDE). The $\dagger$ marks sample-limited test sets ($n \leq 20$) where effect sizes are descriptive rather than confirmatory. Had we reported only CR-composite-layer results, we would have concluded a scale-dependent HS advantage that is entirely a methodological artifact. A random-label control on QwQ-32B confirms that the crossing-rate shallow-layer bias is a geometric property of the representations (100\% of random-label repeats select shallow layers), while threshold-based deep-layer selection requires real safety labels (\cref{app:random_cp}). AUROC, excluded from our primary metrics because it is threshold-free (\cref{sec:evaluation}), confirms HS discriminability at BA-selected layers ($\Delta$AUROC +12.1 to +15.1pp; \cref{tab:ba_layer_results}) but cannot diagnose the threshold-dependent layer selection bias.
40	
41	\subsection{HS vs.\ Text Comparison}\label{sec:hs-text}
42	
43	\begin{table}[t]
44	\centering
45	\small
46	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
47	\begin{tabular}{llclrrlrc}
48	\toprule
49	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Layer} & \textbf{Enc.} & $W$ & $\Delta$\textbf{BA} & $\Delta$\textbf{Prec} & \textbf{95\% CI} & $\Delta$\textbf{FPR} & \textbf{HB} \\
50	\midrule
51	R1-8B & L14 & 384d & 3 & +17.5 & +20.1 & [+12.4, +28.3] & $-$7.9 & \checkmark \\
52	 & & 1024d & & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & +5.8 & [$-$7.4, +19.5] & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & \\[2pt]
53	OT-7B & L16 & 384d & 3 & +10.7 & +21.9 & [+14.4, +29.6] & $-$17.1 & \checkmark \\
54	 & & 1024d & & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & +18.1 & [+8.4, +29.0] & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & \checkmark \\[2pt]
55	QwQ & L63 & 384d & 5 & +13.0 & +19.2 & [+9.3, +33.5] & $-$15.0 & \checkmark \\
56	 & & 1024d & & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & +9.4 & [$-$7.1, +27.7] & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & \\[2pt]
57	R1-32B & L63 & 384d & 1 & +18.7 & +15.4 & [+8.7, +22.6] & $-$14.6 & \checkmark \\
58	 & & 1024d & & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & +11.7 & [$-$0.2, +24.3] & \multicolumn{1}{c}{--} & \\
59	\bottomrule
60	\end{tabular}}
61	\caption{HS vs.\ text at threshold-based layers (LR probes, 60/20/20 split, 10{,}000 bootstrap resamples). Enc.: text encoder (384d = MiniLM-L6-v2, 1024d = BGE-large). $\Delta$: HS$-$text difference (pp); ``--'' = BA and FPR are not computed for the 1024d comparison because the 384d and 1024d encoders operate at different probe calibration points and do not share a decision threshold. HB: \checkmark{} = model-level test passes Holm-Bonferroni ($\alpha{=}0.05$); all 384d model-level tests pass$^\dagger$. 1024d: HB over 4 model-level precision tests.}
62	\label{tab:hs_vs_text}
63	\end{table}
64	
65	The HS advantage is encoder-conditional: against BGE-large (1024d), only OT-7B survives HB correction (\cref{app:encoder_robustness}). Multi-seed stability appears in \cref{app:multi_seed}. Against the 384d baseline, HS probes outperform text probes in all four models$^\dagger$ (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}): confirmatory at 7--8B (OT-7B: +21.9pp precision, R1-8B: +20.1pp), significant but position-competitive at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp), and exploratory at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp, position-mediated). R1-8B FPR is directionally consistent (5/5 seeds) but not robust: $p{=}0.044$ (rank 12/12 in the HB step-down, the weakest surviving test), with only 1/5 seeds passing Bonferroni correction (\cref{app:multi_seed}). R1-32B passes 5/5 seeds ($\Delta$Prec std${=}2.0$pp) but its advantage is position-mediated (residualized gap NS; \cref{app:position_residual}); QwQ-32B's position baseline is competitive (\cref{sec:32b-analysis}). Overall, 18/20 model-seed combinations pass full HB (\cref{app:multi_seed}). Control task selectivity confirms genuine safety signal: 11.1--16.8pp above chance (\cref{app:control}); selectivity measures label structure (main vs.\ shuffled), complementary to position contribution (temporal artifacts). Position features account for 9--20pp of balanced accuracy (\cref{app:position_residual}); R1-32B's HS advantage is fully explained by position (residualized gap +1.9pp, $p{=}0.914$).
66	
67	\paragraph{Capacity control.} PCA reduction of HS features to 384d (79--92\% variance retained) preserves the precision advantage across all four models$^\dagger$ (+16.8 to +23.1pp, all $p{<}0.012$, all HB). Two individual metrics are non-significant: R1-8B BA (+1.3pp, $p{=}0.731$) and QwQ-32B FPR ($-$11.4pp, $p{=}0.038$, below HB threshold). The control provides partial evidence against a pure capacity explanation but does not rule out representation quality differences. Random projection to 384d yields similar results ($\Delta$Prec +8.3 to +20.5pp; \cref{app:random_projection}), further weakening the capacity explanation. E5-Mistral-7B (4096d$\rightarrow$PCA 384d) yields intermediate results (2/4 HB; \cref{app:e5_mistral}), forming a monotonic encoder-quality gradient with MiniLM (4/4) and BGE-large (1/4).
68	
69	\paragraph{Encoder robustness.} Against BGE-large~\citep{xiao2023cpack} (1024d), only OT-7B survives HB (1/4 precision); R1-8B shows adverse FPR direction (+1.2pp). The advantage is encoder-conditional (\cref{fig:forest_precision}); layer selection (Contribution 1) is encoder-independent.
70	
71	\paragraph{Position mediation.} Position ($t/T$) accounts for 9--20pp of balanced accuracy,\footnote{R1-32B's 20.4pp drop reflects $W{=}1$; at $W{\geq}3$, drops are 9--17pp.} but all models retain non-positional signal above chance (all $p{<}0.001$; \cref{app:position_residual}). Three of four models retain significant non-positional HS advantage (residualized gap +3.7 to +6.9pp, HB corrected); R1-32B's gap is +1.9pp ($p{=}0.914$, $n{=}20$). Adding a quadratic position term $(t/T)^2$ does not change significance conclusions for the 7--8B models. However, QwQ-32B's advantage is fully absorbed by the quadratic term (\cref{tab:position_quadratic}), suggesting its residualized advantage contains a non-linear position component. This sensitivity, combined with R1-32B's non-significance under linear control, indicates that 32B position mediation results should be interpreted cautiously. Temporal windowing reduces position dependence (24.3pp drop at $W{=}3$ vs.\ 16.5pp at $W{=}15$).
72	
73	\paragraph{Caveats.} Nested 5-fold cross-validation confirms the HS precision advantage for both 7--8B models (10/10 folds; \cref{app:nested_cv}), with shrinkage of 13--25\% relative to holdout estimates, ruling out hyperparameter overfitting. OT-7B nested CV selects L21--27 vs.\ holdout L16 vs.\ CR-composite L0; the +21.9pp holdout estimate is an upper bound, and the nested CV shrunk estimate is the conservative reference. This inconsistency itself supports Contribution~1 (layer selection sensitivity). R1-32B achieves significance only at $W{=}1$ with 25\% coverage; at $W{\geq}3$, dimensionality prevents significance. Regularization $C \in [0.01, 100]$ yields ${<}2$pp BA variation; decision thresholds are similarly stable (\cref{app:threshold_sensitivity}). QwQ-32B HS lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps): higher precision at later detection. False alarm rates remain 11--50\%, so current methods characterize the phenomenon rather than constitute production detectors. Per-model details in \cref{sec:32b-analysis}.
74	
75	\subsection{32B Model-Specific Analysis}\label{sec:32b-analysis}
76	
77	Both 32B results are exploratory ($n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, as each fold would contain only 4 traces per class). We report effect sizes as descriptive rather than confirmatory; LOO-CV and multi-seed analyses (\cref{app:layer_sweep,app:multi_seed}) provide partial robustness checks but do not substitute for independent validation. By contrast, nested CV on the 7--8B models shows 13--25\% shrinkage (\cref{app:nested_cv}), confirming those estimates. R1-32B and QwQ-32B share the Qwen-32B architecture (64 layers, 5120 hidden) but present opposite detection profiles (\cref{tab:32b_divergence}); training method is the likely differentiator.
78	
79	\begin{table}[t]
80	\centering
81	\small
82	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
83	\toprule
84	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Cov.} & \textbf{Lead (steps)} & \textbf{HB} & \textbf{Pos.\ margin} \\
85	\midrule
86	R1-32B & 25\% & +11.7 to +13.3 & \checkmark{} ($W{=}1$) & +14.2pp \\
87	QwQ-32B & 74\% & $-$1.2 to +1.9 & \checkmark{} (all $W$) & $-$3.6pp \\
88	\bottomrule
89	\end{tabular}
90	\caption{32B cross-model divergence. R1-32B provides limited early detection with narrow coverage; QwQ-32B provides robust significance with poor lead time. HB: \checkmark{} = model-level test passes Holm-Bonferroni ($\alpha{=}0.05$). Pos.\ margin: HS balanced accuracy minus position-only baseline.}
91	\label{tab:32b_divergence}
92	\end{table}
93	
94	R1-32B detects commitment 11--13 steps early (+14.2pp over position baseline) but covers only 25\% of traces ($W{=}1$). QwQ-32B achieves significance at all window sizes with 74\% coverage but negative HS lead time. QwQ-32B's position baseline achieves higher BA (0.832 vs.\ 0.796); HS precision (+4.5pp, $p{=}0.133$) and FPR margins are not significant at $n{=}19$; MDE at 80\% power is 8.6--9.5pp (\cref{app:power_analysis}). The divergence implies per-model validation is essential: no single configuration generalizes even within the same architecture at the same scale.
95	
96	\subsection{Temporal Context}\label{sec:temporal}
